`SequenceMatcher` builds its matching blocks by repeatedly finding the longest contiguous run that `a` and `b` share, then recursing on what lies to the left and to the right of it. Junk and autojunk both work by removing elements from the index used to find those runs, which changes which runs can be found.

**How blocks are picked.** `get_matching_blocks` starts with the whole of `a` and `b` and asks `find_longest_match` for the single longest contiguous block `a[i:i+k] == b[j:j+k]`. It records that block, then does the same for the region left of it (`a[alo:i]` vs `b[blo:j]`) and the region right of it, using an explicit queue instead of recursion. At the end it sorts the blocks, merges any that turned out to be adjacent, and appends the `(len(a), len(b), 0)` sentinel.

Because each match pins an anchor and later matches must fall entirely on one side of it, the blocks are always in increasing order in both sequences. This is greedy, so it does not give a minimal edit script or a longest common subsequence. One long match chosen early can rule out several shorter ones that would have totalled more.

**How the longest match is found.** `__chain_b` precomputes `b2j`, a map from each element of `b` to the list of positions where it occurs. `find_longest_match` walks `a` one element at a time, keeping `j2len[j]` = the length of the match ending at `a[i-1]` and `b[j]`. For each occurrence `j` of `a[i]` in `b`, the new length is `j2len[j-1] + 1`. Ties go to the block starting earliest in `a`, then earliest in `b`, because the best is only replaced on a strictly longer match.

**What junk does.** If you pass `isjunk`, every element of `b` for which it returns true is deleted from `b2j` and remembered in `bjunk`. Since the main loop only sees elements in `b2j`, a junk element can never start or be inside the core match. After the core match is found, it is extended in two steps:

1. It grows outward over matching non-junk elements (this matters for popular elements, below).
2. It then grows outward over matching junk elements that happen to be adjacent.

So junk is never the reason two regions are aligned, but identical junk next to a real match is absorbed into it. That is why, with blanks as junk, `" abcd"` vs `"abcd abcd"` matches the first `abcd` instead of the `" abcd"` at the end. If a region has no non-junk match at all, the core match is empty at `(alo, blo)` and only the junk extension can grow it, so junk there matches only if it sits right at the start of both regions.

**What autojunk does.** When `autojunk=True` (the default) and `b` has at least 200 elements, any non-junk element occurring more than `len(b) // 100 + 1` times is also deleted from `b2j` and recorded in `bpopular`. This is mainly a speed measure: the inner loop runs once per occurrence in `b` of each element of `a`, so very common elements (blank lines, `return NULL;`) dominate the cost.

Popular elements are not in `bjunk`, so they behave differently from real junk: they cannot seed a match, but the first extension step picks them up when they are adjacent to a seeded match. A run made only of popular elements, with nothing rarer nearby, will not be matched at all.

**Effects on the result worth knowing.**

- **Lower `ratio()` on long, repetitive input:** when comparing long strings character by character, almost every character can be "popular", so few matches are seeded and near-identical sequences can score very low. Passing `autojunk=False` fixes this at a cost in speed.
- **Asymmetry:** both junk and popularity are computed from `b` only, so swapping `a` and `b` can give different blocks and a different ratio.
- **`quick_ratio()` and `real_quick_ratio()` ignore junk:** they count over the full sequences, so they remain upper bounds on `ratio()` but can be much higher than it.

`limit_denominator` works because it walks the continued-fraction expansion of the value, which produces the only fractions that can be the closest one under a denominator cap. Plain rounding answers a different question: the best fraction with one specific denominator, not with any denominator up to the limit.

**What the loop computes.** The loop is Euclid's algorithm on `n, d` (starting from the numerator and denominator), and each quotient `a = n//d` is the next continued-fraction term. Alongside it, `p0/q0` and `p1/q1` are the two most recent convergents, built by the standard recurrence `p2 = p0 + a*p1`, `q2 = q0 + a*q1`. The loop stops when the next convergent's denominator `q2` would exceed `max_denominator`. At that point `p1/q1` is the last convergent that fits.

**The two candidates.** The last convergent is not always the answer, because a full step of `a` may overshoot the limit while a partial step still fits. So `k = (max_denominator - q0)//q1` is the largest partial step allowed, giving the semiconvergent `(p0 + k*p1)/(q0 + k*q1)`. For `3.141592653589793` with limit 100, the convergents are 3, 22/7, 333/106. Since 106 is too big, `k = 14` gives (3 + 14·22)/(1 + 14·7) = 311/99, which beats 22/7 and matches the docstring.

**Why one of those two must be the best.** Three facts carry the argument:

- **They bracket the value:** `p1/q1` lies on one side of `self` and the semiconvergent on the other.
- **They are neighbours:** consecutive convergents satisfy `p0*q1 - p1*q0 = ±1`, and that still holds after adding `k` copies of `p1/q1`. So the candidates are exactly `1/(q1*(q0+k*q1))` apart.
- **Nothing fits between them:** any fraction strictly between two such neighbours has a denominator of at least the sum of theirs, `q0 + (k+1)*q1`, which exceeds the limit by the choice of `k`.

So every other fraction with an allowed denominator lies outside that bracket, and is farther from `self` than the candidate on its side. The `±1` property also means both candidates are already in lowest terms, which is why `_from_coprime_ints` is safe.

**The final comparison.** The loop maintains `|p1*D - q1*N| = d`, where `N/D` is `self`, so the distance from `p1/q1` to `self` is `d/(q1*D)`. The convergent wins when that distance is at most half the gap between the candidates, which simplifies to the integer test `2*d*(q0+k*q1) <= self._denominator`. On a tie the `<=` picks `p1/q1`, the one with the smaller denominator.

**Why not just round.** There are two ways to "just round", and neither holds up:

- **Round at the limit:** `round(x * M) / M` gives the best fraction with denominator exactly `M`. For pi with limit 10 that is 31/10 (off by about 0.04), while 22/7 is off by about 0.001.
- **Round at every denominator:** trying each `q` from 1 to `M` and keeping the best is correct but takes `M` steps, a million with the default limit. The loop takes a number of steps logarithmic in the limit, because convergent denominators grow at least as fast as Fibonacci numbers.

The loop also stays entirely in exact integer arithmetic, so the result is not affected by float rounding even for huge numerators and denominators.

**`firstweekday`** only changes which weekday sits in column 0 of `monthdayscalendar`; the day numbers themselves are the same. That changes how many zeros pad the first row (`(day1 - firstweekday) % 7`) and the last row, so it also shifts where weeks break and can change the number of rows (4 to 6).

The `Calendar` property reduces the value mod 7 on read, so `Calendar(7)` silently behaves as Monday. The module-level `setfirstweekday()` instead rejects anything outside 0–6.

**`itermonthdates` at the edges** is the surprising part: it builds a `datetime.date` for every padding day too, so it can fail on a month that is itself valid. I worked these cases out from the code and did not run them.

- **January of year 1:** 1 January 0001 is a Monday, so with the default `firstweekday=0` there is no leading padding and it works. With any other first weekday it needs days from December of year 0 and raises `ValueError` on the first `next()`.
- **December 9999:** 31 December 9999 is a Friday, so with the default it needs 1–2 January 10000 as trailing padding. Because it is a generator, it yields every valid date first and only then raises `ValueError`. It works only with `firstweekday=5` (Saturday), where no trailing padding is needed.
- **Knock-on failures:** `monthdatescalendar(9999, 12)` and `yeardatescalendar(9999)` raise under the default setting, since they consume the whole iterator.
- **Other iterators are unaffected:** `itermonthdays`, `itermonthdays2`, `itermonthdays3` and `itermonthdays4` never build a `date` for padding. `weekday()` maps out-of-range years to `2000 + year % 400`, so they work even for year 0 or 10000; `itermonthdays3`/`4` are the workaround at the boundaries.

`python3 roster.py inactive` now lists every learner whose last login was 14 or more days ago, in the same format as `list` (id, name, email, courses). Run against the current data today, it prints Ben Whitlock and Dara Novak.

I checked the boundary: a learner whose last login was exactly 14 days ago is included, and one at 13 days is not. The threshold is the `INACTIVE_AFTER_DAYS` constant at the top of `roster.py`, and I added the command to the usage text and the README.

The output does not show the last-login date itself, since it reuses the existing listing format; say if you want that column added for the nudge emails.
